language_wrapper: There are {alpha} piles of coins S_1, S_2, ..., S_{alpha}. For each prime p listed in the mapping [prime_quotas], pile S_k initially contains exactly r_p coins labeled p if and only if p divides k, and contains none of that label otherwise (here r_p is the value associated to p in [prime_quotas]). An operation selects an ordered triple (i, j, p) satisfying: 1 <= i < j <= {alpha}, p is a prime key of [prime_quotas], p divides both i and j, each of S_i and S_j currently has at least one coin labeled p, and the triple (i, j, p) has not been selected before. The operation removes one coin labeled p from each of S_i and S_j. What is the maximum number of operations that can be performed?
hardness_rationale: The seed problem couples gcd-based removals across dynamic pile sizes, which can be approached with number-theoretic invariants. Our family introduces prime-labeled budgets and triple operations (i, j, p) that decompose the process per prime into constrained edge packings on complete graphs of multiples of p. Determining the maximum operations now requires understanding and proving optimality of degree-constrained edge packings on complete graphs for each prime and summing contributions, invoking concepts from graph realization (Havel–Hakimi/Erdős–Gallai) and constructive regular/near-regular graph existence. This elevates the difficulty from purely number-theoretic gcd manipulation to an interplay of multiplicative structure and extremal graph theory with rigorous capacity arguments.
notes: Proof sketch: Fix a prime p with m = floor(alpha/p) vertices (the multiples of p). Each operation using p consumes 1 unit of p-budget at each endpoint, and each unordered pair can be used at most once, so the subproblem is: maximize the number of edges E_p in a simple graph on m vertices with per-vertex degree upper bound r_p. A trivial upper bound is min(C(m,2), floor(m*r_p/2)). We claim this bound is tight. If m*r_p is even, an r_p-regular simple graph on m vertices exists for any 0 <= r_p <= m-1 (construct via circulant graphs or by decomposing K_m into 1-factors and combining). Hence E_p = m*r_p/2. If m*r_p is odd, take an almost-regular degree sequence (r_p, ..., r_p, r_p - 1); its sum is m*r_p - 1 (even), and it is graphic for m >= 2 and r_p <= m - 1 (again realizable by adjusting a regular construction or Havel–Hakimi). Thus E_p = floor(m*r_p/2). Since operations for distinct primes consume disjoint labeled budgets and triples are uniquely identified by (i, j, p), the total maximum equals sum_p E_p = sum_p floor((alpha//p) * r_p / 2). This preserves the coin-pile framework while requiring advanced reasoning about degree-constrained subgraphs. Implementation notes: The generator only selects primes p <= alpha//2 so m_p >= 2, and ensures at least one prime has m_p >= 3 and r_p >= 2. The verifier checks primality, bounds, and computes the sum floor(m_p * r_p / 2) as the answer.
source_question: There are 7671 piles of coins, denoted as \(S_1, S_2, \cdots, S_{7671}\) respectively. Initially, for each \(k = 1, 2, \cdots, 7671\), there are \(k\) coins in the pile \(S_k\). In one operation, an ordered pair \((i, j)\) is selected, where \(i\) and \(j\) satisfy the following two conditions: - \(1\leq i < j\leq7671\); - There is at least one coin in both the pile \(S_i\) and the pile \(S_j\); - The ordered pair \((i, j)\) has not been selected in any previous operation. Then, if there are \(a\) coins and \(b\) coins in \(S_i\) and \(S_j\) respectively, \(\gcd(a,b)\) coins are removed from each of the two piles. What is the maximum number of times this operation can be performed?
